title: Android Kotlin Coroutines
description: Beginner-to-advanced guide to structured concurrency, dispatchers, cancellation, errors, synchronization, bounded concurrency, callback interop, lifecycle scopes, and production coroutine design on Android.

sections.title: Coroutine Foundations
sections.description: Separate suspension, concurrency, parallelism, and threads.

subtopics.title: Suspending Is Not Blocking
subtopics.description: A suspend function may pause without occupying its thread. The continuation later resumes on a dispatcher; suspend does not automatically mean background execution.

annotations.text: Allows suspension; it does not choose a thread or start a coroutine.

callouts.title: Main-Safe APIs
callouts.text: Every suspend function should be safe to call from the main thread. Move blocking or CPU-heavy implementation details inside the function with an injected dispatcher.

callouts.title: Coroutine ≠ Thread
callouts.text: Many coroutines can share a small thread pool. A coroutine can resume on a different thread unless its dispatcher confines it.

subtopics.title: launch, async & withContext
subtopics.description: launch returns Job for work without a result; async returns Deferred for concurrent results; withContext switches context and returns a result without creating unstructured work.

tabs.label: Launch
tabs.code:
val job: Job = scope.launch { repository.refresh() }
job.join() // wait; failure follows parent/handler rules

tabs.label: Async
withContext
tabs.code:
suspend fun parse(bytes: ByteArray): Model =
    withContext(defaultDispatcher) { parser.parse(bytes) }

callouts.title: Do Not Use async for Sequential Work
callouts.text: Calling await immediately after each async removes concurrency and adds complexity. Use direct suspend calls unless operations are independent and should overlap.

sections.title: Structured Concurrency & Ownership
sections.description: Every coroutine should have a clear parent, lifetime, cancellation path, and failure policy.

subtopics.title: Job Trees & Parent-Child Rules
subtopics.description: A parent waits for its children. Parent cancellation cancels children; an ordinary child failure cancels its parent and siblings.

diagram.content:
flowchart TD
  P[Parent scope] --> A[Child A]
  P --> B[Child B]
  B --> C[Grandchild]
  X[Cancel parent] -.-> P
  P -. cancellation .-> A
  P -. cancellation .-> B
  B -. cancellation .-> C

callouts.title: Avoid GlobalScope
callouts.text: GlobalScope detaches work from caller lifetime and error handling. Inject an application-level scope only for work that intentionally outlives the screen, or use WorkManager for durable deferrable work.

subtopics.title: coroutineScope vs supervisorScope
subtopics.description: coroutineScope fails the whole operation when any child fails. supervisorScope isolates child failures, but each failure still needs explicit handling.

callouts.title: Supervision Is a Product Decision
callouts.text: Use supervision only when partial success is meaningful. If results must be consistent as a unit, regular coroutineScope is the safer invariant.

subtopics.title: Work That Outlives a Screen
subtopics.description: Inject a longer-lived scope when completion matters after navigation, and join it when the caller must wait for the outcome.

callouts.title: Use WorkManager for Durable Work
callouts.text: An application process can die. Use WorkManager when work must eventually run under constraints or survive process recreation; an application coroutine scope cannot provide durability.

sections.title: Dispatchers & Coroutine Context
sections.description: Choose execution resources based on work type and inject them for deterministic tests.

subtopics.title: Main, IO, Default & Limited Parallelism
subtopics.description: Main is for UI; IO for blocking I/O; Default for CPU-heavy work. limitedParallelism bounds concurrency for a resource without creating an unmanaged executor.

table.title: Dispatcher Selection Guide
rows: Run immediately when already on Main
Using it as a general performance shortcut
Avoid an extra dispatch in tightly controlled UI code
Blocking file, socket, and legacy database calls
Decode or sort a large dataset
Bound access to a scarce resource
Assuming it creates a dedicated thread
Limit concurrent uploads or database work
Hard-coding production dispatchers in domain code

callouts.title: IO Is Not Faster CPU
callouts.text: Dispatchers.IO permits more blocking tasks; it is not the correct pool for expensive computation. Excess CPU work on IO can still starve the device.

subtopics.title: Inject Dispatchers & Scopes
subtopics.description: Constructor-injected execution dependencies make ownership visible and let tests share one virtual-time scheduler.

callouts.title: Do Not Hide Ownership
callouts.text: Prefer receiving a scope from the component that owns the lifetime. Creating CoroutineScope inside arbitrary classes makes cancellation and failure policies difficult to audit.

sections.title: Cancellation, Cleanup & Timeouts
sections.description: Cancellation is cooperative and should remain visible through every layer.

subtopics.title: Make CPU & Blocking Work Cancellable
subtopics.description: Suspending kotlinx.coroutines APIs check cancellation. Tight CPU loops and blocking calls must check or provide their own cancellation mechanism.

callouts.title: Never Swallow CancellationException
callouts.text: A broad catch can convert cancellation into success and keep obsolete work running. Rethrow CancellationException, or catch only the domain failures you can handle.

subtopics.title: finally, use & NonCancellable
subtopics.description: Use finally/use for cleanup. Enter NonCancellable only for a short suspending cleanup that truly must finish.

callouts.title: Keep NonCancellable Tiny
callouts.text: Large NonCancellable blocks make owners unable to stop work promptly. Do not wrap the main operation merely to force completion.

subtopics.title: withTimeout & withTimeoutOrNull
subtopics.description: Timeouts cancel the enclosed coroutine. Decide whether timeout is exceptional or an expected absence.

callouts.title: Timeout Does Not Stop Uncooperative APIs
callouts.text: Cancellation stops the coroutine only when the underlying operation cooperates. Wrap callback APIs so cancellation unregisters callbacks or invokes the platform cancellation signal.

sections.title: Exceptions & Failure Policy
sections.description: Know where exceptions propagate, where they are observed, and where recovery belongs.

subtopics.title: launch vs async Exceptions
subtopics.description: Root launch reports uncaught failures; async stores failure until await, but a failing child still cancels its regular parent immediately.

callouts.title: Handle Expected Failures Near the Use Case
callouts.text: Convert network, validation, and storage failures into domain outcomes where meaningful. Keep global handlers for logging unexpected root failures, not routine recovery.

subtopics.title: CoroutineExceptionHandler
subtopics.description: A handler observes uncaught exceptions of root coroutines. It does not catch exceptions so execution can resume and does not handle awaited Deferred failures.

codeBlocks.code:
val handler = CoroutineExceptionHandler { context, error ->
    crashReporter.record(error, context[CoroutineName]?.name)
}
val appScope = CoroutineScope(SupervisorJob() + Dispatchers.Default + handler)

callouts.title: Not a try/catch Replacement
callouts.text: Use structured try/catch around operations that have a fallback. CoroutineExceptionHandler is a last-chance observer for uncaught root failures.

sections.title: Android Lifecycle Scopes
sections.description: Start work in the component that owns its useful lifetime.

subtopics.title: viewModelScope
subtopics.description: Use viewModelScope for screen business logic that should survive configuration changes and stop when the ViewModel is cleared.

callouts.title: Views Delegate Business Work
callouts.text: Activities and composables should normally send user actions to the ViewModel. This survives configuration changes and keeps business logic unit-testable.

subtopics.title: lifecycleScope & repeatOnLifecycle
subtopics.description: Use lifecycleScope for UI-related work. Use repeatOnLifecycle for ongoing work that must stop while the UI is not visible.

callouts.title: Flow Details Live Elsewhere
callouts.text: See Android Kotlin Flows for StateFlow, SharedFlow, sharing, operators, and lifecycle-aware collection patterns.

sections.title: Synchronization, Interop & Performance
sections.description: Protect shared state without blocking threads and diagnose concurrency problems.

subtopics.title: Mutex, Atomic Updates & Confinement
subtopics.description: Prefer immutable state and ownership. Use Mutex for suspendable critical sections, atomics for simple lock-free values, or a single owner/dispatcher for confinement.

callouts.title: No Suspending I/O Under Broad Locks
callouts.text: A Mutex suspends rather than blocks, but a long critical section still serializes callers. Keep invariants narrow and avoid cyclic lock acquisition.

subtopics.title: Bridge One-Shot Callbacks
subtopics.description: Use suspendCancellableCoroutine and unregister or cancel the platform operation when the coroutine is cancelled.

callouts.title: Resume Exactly Once
callouts.text: Callback APIs can fire repeatedly or race with cancellation. Guard one-shot completion and unregister promptly; use callbackFlow for multi-shot streams.

subtopics.title: Bounded Concurrency & Rate Limits
subtopics.description: Bound concurrent work to device and service capacity. A coroutine per item is cheap to create but the I/O, memory, sockets, and remote quota it consumes are not free.

callouts.title: Retries Multiply Load
callouts.text: Combine bounded concurrency with retry limits, jittered backoff, idempotency, and server guidance. Unbounded fan-out plus synchronized retries can amplify an outage.

subtopics.title: Debugging & Production Checklist
subtopics.description: Name important coroutines and audit every lifetime, dispatcher, and failure boundary.

codeBlocks.code:
□ Every launched coroutine has an intentional owner
□ Suspend APIs are main-safe
□ Dispatchers and long-lived scopes are injected
□ Independent work uses async only when concurrency helps
□ Fan-out is bounded to device/service capacity
□ Retries are bounded, jittered, and safe to repeat
□ CancellationException is never swallowed
□ CPU loops check cancellation
□ Child failure versus supervision matches product semantics
□ Blocking calls run on IO; CPU work runs on Default
□ Large inputs are streamed or explicitly size-bounded
□ Shared mutable state has one owner or synchronization
□ Callback bridges unregister and complete atomically once
□ Durable work uses WorkManager
□ Tests use one TestCoroutineScheduler

callouts.title: Name Long-Lived Work
callouts.text: CoroutineName plus structured logging makes job dumps and crash reports far easier to understand. Measure before adding concurrency; more coroutines can increase contention and battery use.
